outputs.key: Find everything a plant has let go of this month. Seeds, nuts, cones, keys, berries.
Pick one. What is yours wearing?
How did yours get from up there down to here?
Hold it as high as you can and let it go. Watch what it does.
What a seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling.
Walk under the trees and bring back one fallen leaf. Choose it for its colour.
Lay your leaf in the line. Greenest at this end, brownest at that end.
Where do you think the green goes?
The yellow was there all along. The green was just sitting on top of it.
Look at the end of your stalk. Can you find where the tree let it go?
Every autumn every tree drops every leaf it has. So why is our playground not buried in leaves?
Where do you think they all go?
Lift the leaves and look underneath. Who is living down here?
Who did you find?
What was it doing to the leaf?
Look for white threads running through the wet leaves. That is a fungus, and it is eating too.
Dig down to where the leaves stop looking like leaves. Rub some between your fingers.
That was leaves. Now it is soil. Everything growing here is growing in it.
Stand still. Put a stone where your shadow ends.
The sun is getting lower every day. Your shadow will be longer next time we do this.
Hunt for somebody who is getting ready for the cold. Look for what they have left behind.
Four answers to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground.
Which answer did the one you found choose?
The cold is coming for us too. What do we do about it?
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?

Something has been changing our garden. It came quietly, without asking anyone. Today you are detectives, and your job is to find the evidence. Real detectives use everything: eyes, ears, hands, noses.
Walk slowly. When you find a clue, stop and really meet it. Is it a colour? A sound? Something under your shoes? Collect it if the ground gives it to you, and point it out if it is still attached.
Now close your eyes for a moment where you stand. What can you hear? What can you smell? Detectives trust every sense.
Find one clue nobody else has found yet. The best detectives look where nobody else is looking: up high, down low, underneath.
Today the weather itself is a clue. Rain is one of autumn's helpers. Find a puddle that was not here in summer. Find where the water goes. Smell the air: rain wakes the smell of the soil.
Draw your favourite clue. It does not need to be neat. It needs to be yours.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
First force: the earth itself. Dig gently and see what the ground is keeping: roots, stones, seeds, old leaves turning dark, maybe someone small and alive.
Who lives in the soil? Look under the leaves lying on top too. The dark crumbly bits were leaves once. Something is turning them into soil.
Second force: the air. You cannot see wind, but your ribbon can. Hold it up. Where does it dance hardest? Go and find the windiest place in our garden.
Now the opposite hunt: find a place where your ribbon goes completely to sleep. Somewhere the wind cannot reach.
Watch a tree in the wind. Does the trunk move, or just the branches and leaves? Which parts of the tree does the wind win against?
Make a wind map in your head: strongest place, stillest place. Why is the still place still? What is standing between it and the wind?
Third force: water. Find its fingerprints: a puddle, dark damp soil, drops still holding onto a leaf. Feel a wet leaf and a dry leaf. What has the water changed?

We do not have to imagine this force today: it is working right now. Hold out a hand and catch some. Follow a trickle. Find where the garden's water likes to collect, and smell the air while you are there.
The three forces have repainted our garden. Last hunt of the day: find autumn's warm colours. Red, orange, yellow, gold, brown. Bring back one small fallen thing for each colour you can.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?

Here is a fresh leaf. Every autumn, thousands like it fall here. So why are we not buried in leaves up to the windows? Somewhere between falling and disappearing, something happens to every single leaf. Today we find out what.
What do you think this leaf will look like by spring?

The leaf-eaters are hiding right under our feet. Lift the wet leaves gently. Look beside the logs and in the dark damp places. Worms, woodlice, beetles, and the little threads of fungi: this is the recycling crew.
We have met the recycling crew. Now we build them a restaurant, in layers, like a lasagne. Watch how one layer goes on, then we all build together.
The restaurant is open. Draw our compost in your journal exactly as it looks today, because it will not stay like this. We will visit every week and catch it changing.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?

Every laboratory needs ingredients, and ours are lying on the ground: fallen leaves, dropped petals, grass, a twig, a seed, one pinch of soil. Only what the ground gives. Nothing gets picked, and nothing goes near our mouths.
Before anything touches the water: scientists guess first, out loud, on purpose. Hold up your leaf. Float or sink? Say it.
Now the rest of your ingredients. Your twig: float or sink? Your seed? Your pinch of soil?
And the big one: will anything change the water's colour? Lock your guess in.
There is no wrong guess before the test. There is only what the water says afterwards.
Make one prediction you are sure of and one you are truly not sure of. The unsure one is the better experiment. Why?
Say what you see, like a scientist: it floats, it sinks, the water is turning brown, the leaf feels different now it is wet. What actually happened? Was the water right, or were you?
Now let your potion rest while we tidy the lab. At the very end, come back for one last look: what changed while you were not watching?
Every great potion needs a name and a power. Look at what you actually made: its colour, what floats in it, how it moves. Let the potion tell you its name.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?

Today the garden feeds us. First job: what here can actually be eaten, and is it ready? For everything we gather, one question: which part of the plant are we holding? A root? A leaf? A fruit? A seed?
How did this food get here? Someone planted a seed, the plant grew all summer, and autumn finished it. We are eating months of work.
Sort the harvest into plant parts: roots together, leaves together, fruits together. Which team has the most? Which food was the hardest to place?
Cooks count and cooks measure. How many apples went in? Is the bowl half full or nearly whole? Do we have more red pieces or more green?
The cooks eat together. Before we do: how do we share this so it is fair? Count the cups, count the cooks. Fair means everyone gets their share of what everyone made.

One last job, and it closes a circle: the peels and ends go to our compost. The recycling crew turns them into soil, the soil feeds the plants, and the plants will feed us again. Seed, plant, harvest, food, scraps, soil, seed. Round and round.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
Imagine you had to spend the whole winter outside, right here. No house, no shops, no coat cupboard. What would you need? Think, then tell me your survival plan.

The garden's animals are solving this puzzle right now, and they have different plans. Some store food and stay busy all winter. Some eat and eat now, then sleep the winter away in a super-sleep called hibernation.
Some birds fly away to warmer places. And many small creatures just find a safe crack or a leaf pile and wait quietly for spring. Four plans: store, sleep, fly, hide.
Time to shop like an animal. What food is the garden still offering? Seeds, berries, fallen fruit, insects hiding in the leaves. Fill your imaginary larder.
Larder full? Now find your winter bedroom: a place that is dry, hidden and out of the wind. Remember where the ribbons went to sleep.
Found a good winter bedroom? Do not touch it or move in: somebody real may already have. Point it out and tell us what makes it good.
Rate your winter bedroom like an animal estate agent: is it dry? Hidden? Out of the wind? Near food? Score it out of four and defend your score.

We know what the animals need, so let us actually help. Leaf piles are winter duvets: beetles, and in some gardens bigger sleepers too, spend all winter inside them. Logs are apartment blocks for small creatures. Our job is to build them and then leave them alone.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
Detectives, one last walk through the case, and bring your journal: it remembers September better than we do. First stop, the compost. What has changed? What has disappeared? Who is visiting?
Second stop: past the winter homes we built, looking from a distance like polite neighbours. Any signs that somebody moved in?
Quick visit in the rain, and notice: the rain is watering our compost for us. One look each: name one thing that has changed since we built it. Then we take the season indoors.

Every piece of our season goes on the floor: leaves falling, leaves hiding creatures, the recycling crew at work, new soil, plants growing from it, plants feeding animals and feeding us, the seasons turning, winter on its way. Now, how do the pieces join? Let us build it as a circle and see.

Last job of the season: our shared display, called Our autumn garden. Every detective contributes their single favourite discovery: a drawing, a journal page, a pressed leaf, a sentence we write down for you. When it is up, it is the whole season, made by all of us.
Before we go out, let's be still for a moment. Take one slow breath with me. Today we're going to meet the trees that live near us, and get to know their leaves.
When a leaf on the ground catches your eye, say hello to it. Notice its shape, its edges, its colour. If you like it, it can come with us in your basket.
When a leaf catches your eye, pick it up and get to know it. Trace its edge with your finger. Does its shape remind you of a tree you already know? Collect the leaves you could introduce to a friend.
Rain makes the colours deeper. Let's look under the big trees, where it's drier. Wet leaves shine like they've just been painted. Say hello to the shiniest one you can find.
Choose the leaves that want to be in your picture. Lay them on your card first and move them around. When it looks right to you, glue them down. There's no wrong picture.
Bring your collage to the circle and set it down in front of you where everyone can see it.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.

We are going on a seed hunt today.
What is a seed?
Have you ever found a seed before? What did it look like?
Take ten minutes to search for plants in our grounds.
What can you see on this plant?
Can you find where the seeds are on this plant?
How do plants make their seeds?
Can you see any seeds that have fallen from the trees on the ground?
How do you think this seed arrived here?
The wind is doing the work today. Stand still near a big tree for a moment. Is anything flying?
Now search the ground on the side the wind blows towards. That is where today's seeds land.
In partners, can you collect four types of seed and place them in your pot?
Try to collect different shapes: some winged, some heavy, some feathered, some flat.
Now test how your seed travels with a partner.
Draw your seeds, and write how each one travelled.
Draw your seed. Tell your partner how it travelled.
Seeds travel four ways: on the wind, on water, with animals, or flung out by the plant itself.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
Today, you get to become an animal.
What is your favourite garden animal?
Does it come out in the day, or at night?
Find leaves on the ground. Different colours, shapes and sizes.
Rain makes the leaves shiny. Collect under the big trees where it is drier.
Pour your leaves out. Big ones here, small ones there.
Now by touch: smooth on one side, rough and crackly on the other.
Last one: line up the colours, green to yellow to orange to brown.
Which animal are you going to be?
Look at your teams. Which leaves make the ears? Which make the fur?
Put your mask on. I will go first.
I am a fox. I live in the city. I come out at night to hunt for food. In the day I hide and rest.
Now you. Who are you, and how did you make your mask?
Some animals come out at night, like the fox and the hedgehog. Some come out in the day, like the robin and the squirrel. Hold up your mask if your animal is a night animal.

Be still with me for one breath. Today is a special one: we're going to choose a tree to be our class's own tree. Not just any tree. Ours. We'll visit it again and again, and watch what it does all year.
Let's visit the trees that live here and see which one wants to be ours. Stand under each one. Look up through its branches. Touch its coat. Which tree feels like it belongs to us, and we to it?

We're choosing carefully, like choosing a friend. Visit each tree and gather its clues: how it stands, what its coat feels like, what lives around its feet, what you can see through its branches. Then we'll choose together, and be able to say why.

This is our tree now, so let's greet it properly. Make a ring around it and hold hands. Now come close and lay your hands on its coat. Look all the way up. Be quiet for one breath and listen to what our tree sounds like.
It says: this tree is known.
Every friend has a name. What shall we call our tree? Say your ideas out loud, and let's listen for the name that fits.
Our tree needs a name, like a friend. What shall we call it? Say your idea out loud.
Our tree doesn't mind the rain; it drinks it. Come under its branches and feel how it shelters us. Is it drier here, under our tree? Listen to the rain landing on its leaves above us.
The difference is the tree's roof.
Circle up where we can still see our tree.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
What season is it right now?
How do you know it is autumn?
What happens to a leaf after it falls off a tree?
Do you know what the word decompose means?
How do you think bugs help a leaf break down?
Where do you think the leaf goes once it is all broken down?
Can you find leaves in different stages of decomposition?
Sort five leaves you have found into an order, from just fallen to most decomposed.
Search for signs of decomposition.
Can you find worms, insects or fungi close by?
In nature, nothing is wasted. Fallen leaves break down and return nutrients to the soil, helping new plants grow.
The shredders and the rotters work as a team. Worms and woodlice chew the leaf into bits, fungi finish the job, and the goodness goes back into the soil.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
Do you know the difference between a conker and an acorn?
Which tree do you think a conker comes from? What about an acorn?
Today we are going on a trail to find, sort and measure them.
In pairs, collect conkers and acorns from the ground. As many as you can find.
In pairs, sort your collection into two groups: conkers and acorns.
Now sort them again by size, smallest to largest.
Count how many of each kind you found. Keep your two numbers ready for the class total.
Let us put all our numbers together. Tell me your conkers first, then your acorns.
We've been away all summer. Look around. What's different?
Touch something that grew while we were gone.
This place kept going without us. How does that feel?
Say: I'm back. I noticed you kept going. Thank you.
Stand still. Close your eyes. Where do you feel the wind?
Watch what the wind moves. Leaves? Grass? Your clothes? What else?
The wind touches everything and holds nothing. What does that feel like?
Thank the wind. It carries seeds. It brings rain. It cleans the air.
Look for something that's falling. A leaf. A seed. A petal. Something letting go.
Catch one. Hold it. Feel how light it is. It used to be part of something.
Is letting go sad or brave or both?
Put it down gently. It has somewhere to go. Say: safe travels.
Kneel down. Look at the ground very closely. What is it made of?
Pick up a handful. Smell it. Squeeze it. What does soil feel like?
Everything that ever lived here is in this soil. It's full of endings that became beginnings.
Put it back. Pat it down. Say: thank you for holding everything up.
Look at the trees. Some colours are leaving. Some are arriving. Which ones?
Find a leaf that's halfway. Still some green. Some gold. Hold the moment of change.
Change is happening right now. Right in front of you. Slower than you but it's happening. Can you feel it?
Thank the colours for showing up before they go.
Stand completely still. Listen. What sounds are missing?
Walk slowly. Listen to what is here. What sounds remain?
When things get quiet, you can hear more deeply. What can you hear that you usually miss?
Thank the quiet. It's teaching us to listen.
Autumn is when things get buried. Seeds fall. Bulbs go down. Look for anything being stored.
Find a seed or a nut or a berry. Feel it. This is a promise for next year.
This thing will sleep all winter. Then wake up. Does anything in you need to rest before it can grow?
Bury it gently. Or leave it where something will find it. Say: see you in spring.
Winter is coming. Find the last warm thing you can.
Hold onto it. Feel the warmth. It won't be here much longer.
Everything warm will get cold. Everything cold will get warm again. That's the promise of the year.
Thank the warmth for staying as long as it could. Say: see you in spring.
The leaves are gone. Look up. What can you see that was hidden?
Touch a bare branch. Follow it with your eyes from trunk to tip.
The tree is not dead. It's resting. Can you feel the difference?
Thank the tree for showing us its bones. That takes courage.
Find something that is frozen. Ice on a puddle. Frost on a leaf. Frozen ground.
Touch it. Quickly. What does frozen feel like?
Water became something completely different. Just from cold. What changes you?
Leave the ice. The sun will set it free later. Say: I'll check on you tomorrow.
Most creatures left or hid. But the birds stayed. Find one.
Watch it. What is it doing? Looking for food? Singing? Waiting?
It's cold. Food is scarce. But this bird stayed. What does it mean to stay when it's hard?
Thank you for staying. We see you. We're glad you're here.
Something here is sleeping. A hedgehog. A frog. A beetle. Look for where they might be hiding.
Put your hand near a hiding place. Feel how sheltered it is. Warm? Dry? Protected?
Imagine sleeping for four months. No alarm. No school. Just rest. How would that feel?
Whisper: sleep well. We won't disturb you. See you in spring.
Breathe out slowly. Can you see it? That's your warmth meeting the cold. That's you being alive.
Put your hand in front of your mouth. Feel the warmth. Your body is a furnace.
You are warm in a cold world. That's amazing. Really feel that.
Breathe on your hands. Warm them up. Then put your warm hands on something cold. Share your heat.
Look at the ground. Who has been here before us? Footprints. Paw prints. Trails.
Put your own foot next to a print. How big is it? What shape are its toes? Which way was it going?
Something was here. Right where you're standing. Maybe last night. Maybe this morning. You missed each other.
Leave your own print. Press your hand into the mud. Say: I was here too.
Winter days are short. The shadows are long. Find the darkest spot you can.
Step into the shadow. Feel how different it is from the light. Colder? Damper? Quieter?
We sometimes avoid the dark. But things grow here. Moss. Ferns. Things that love the shade. Can you be okay in the dark?
Thank the dark for what it grows. The light gets all the credit. But the dark works too.
Spring is coming. It's not here yet. But somewhere, there's a sign. Find it.
Touch it. This tiny thing is about to become something much bigger.
We made it through winter. So did this. How does that feel?
Say: I see you. You're early. Thank you for the promise.

Why do flowers matter?
What is pollination?
How do insects help flowers, and flowers help insects?

Find flowers. Find pollinators.
Watch what visits what.

Take some clay. Press it flat.
Add wildflower seeds. Roll it into a ball.
Make two.

Throw one seed bomb here at school, somewhere it can grow.
Take the other home to throw in your local area.

How do wildflowers spread?
Wind, animals, water, people.
How did the flowers in our space get here?

Find flowers. Smell them. Touch the petals.
Look at the colours. How many different kinds?

Pick one flower and look closely.
Where are its seeds? Can you see any seedlings nearby?

How can we help spread seeds?
Why is it important to have many different kinds of wildflowers?

Where do you see art in nature?
Patterns on leaves, colours in flowers, shapes in bark.

Notice colours, shapes and patterns.
Collect petals, leaves, grass. Only what has already fallen.

Put what you collected in your bowl.
Crush it with the stick. Add a tiny bit of water.
Now use your hands to paint on the paper.

Look at the colours on your page.
They came from the ground, from petals, from leaves.
How does it feel to use nature to make art?

What birds live near our school?
Listen. Can you hear any?
Look. Can you see any?

Go into the space.
What food can birds find here naturally?

Work with a partner. Take half an orange.
Scoop out the inside. Tie string to two sides.
Fill it with birdseed and hang it on a tree.

Why is it important to help wildlife in our local area?
What else could we do to make our school a better place for birds?
Stand still. Close your eyes. What do you hear that wasn't here in winter?
Find something that feels alive. Touch it gently.
How does it feel to find something waking up?
Whisper hello to what you found. Welcome it back.
Kneel down. Put your hands on the ground. What's happening under here?
Dig gently with your fingers. What do you find?
All of this is alive under our feet. How does that feel?
Say thank you to the ground. It holds everything up.
Look around. Find something that's opening.
Go close. Touch it gently. What does opening feel like?
Stay with it. Does this make you feel anything?
Before we go, say thank you to what you found. Out loud or inside.
Look up. Look down. Who is building something here?
Watch them work. What are they carrying? Where?
What would it feel like to build your home with your mouth?
Wish them well. Say: good luck with your home.
Find water. A puddle, a drip, a wet leaf. Where did it come from?
Touch the water. Is it cold? Warm? Moving or still?
This water has been everywhere. The sky, the sea, a cloud, and now here.
Thank the rain for coming.
Look around. Green is not one colour. Find a green nobody else has noticed yet.
Pick your favourite green. Go stand next to it.
Why this green? What drew you here?
Give your green a name. Not a plant name. A feeling name.
Find a seed. Any seed. On the ground, on a plant, in the wind.
Hold it in your palm. Feel how small it is. Feel how much is inside.
This tiny thing contains a whole future. Does anything inside you feel like that?
Put it back where it can grow. Wish it well.
Walk slowly. Find three living things you want to thank.
Stand with each one. Really look at it. See what it does.
Why are you grateful for this one?
Say its name and say thank you. Out loud.
Count everything that's alive within ten steps.
What can you see?
What can you hear?
What is telling you it's alive?
What does it mean to be living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?

If you were the size of a woodlouse, where would you hide?
What minibeasts do you know? Can you name them?
What is your favourite minibeast and why?
Take 10 minutes to explore. Look under logs, on leaves, in trees, and up in the sky.
What minibeasts did you find in our grounds?
How did you identify them?
How many legs did they have?
Did they have wings to fly?
Where did they live?
Go back to a quiet spot and thank a minibeast. They play an important part in keeping our planet alive.
Let's go outside to collect leaves and petals from the ground, in a variety of shades and colours.
Take a seat. Using the materials you collected, create a collage of something you saw in nature.
You can cut and stick pieces of leaves into different patterns or shapes.
Perhaps you want to make an insect, a flower, or a landscape?
What did you make?
How did you use your natural materials to create different parts of your piece?
What inspired you in nature to make this?

Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
Walk around your outside space, taking note of all the different trees you can see.
Why are trees so important for our existence (humans)?
What other creatures on our planet need trees to live?
If there were no trees on our planet, would we be alive?
Stand still. Close your eyes. Where do you feel the sun on your body?
Now touch something the sun has been warming all morning.
The sun is feeding everything here. How does it feel to be fed too?
Say thank you to the sun. It came a long way to be here.
Find something that flies. A bee, a butterfly, a hoverfly. Watch where it goes.
Follow it. Slowly. Don't chase. Just walk where it leads.
It visited three flowers in one minute. It's working. What is its job?
Thank you for the work you do. We need you.
It's warm today. Find the coolest place you can.
Sit in it. Feel the air on your skin. What made this cool place?
Something alive made this shelter for you. Does that change how it feels?
Thank what made the shade. Touch it gently before you go.
Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. What can you smell?
Walk slowly. Find the strongest smell you can. Go right up to it.
Does this smell remind you of anything? A place? A person? A feeling?
Breathe it in one more time. Remember it. This is what summer smells like at your school.
Look around. Find something that something eats. A berry. A leaf. A seed. Nectar.
Look closely. Can you see the marks where something has already eaten?
This place is a restaurant for hundreds of creatures. How does that make you feel?
Leave the food where it is. Someone needs it more than we do.
Look at all the colours. Which one is shouting the loudest?
Go to it. Get your eyes really close. What do you see inside?
This flower is trying to be seen. It dressed up for today. Do you ever do that?
Tell the flower: I see you. You're beautiful.
Point to where the sun is now. Point to where it will set tonight.
Find the longest shadow you can. Stand in it. Now find the shortest.
Summer days are the longest days. The light stays late. How does long light make you feel?
Thank the long day for all the light it gives.
Take ten steps. Stop. Now count everything that is alive within arm's reach.
Touch five different living things right where you stand.
You are standing in a crowd of living things. You are never alone outside. How does that feel?
Thank them all. Every single one. Just say: thank you, everyone.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
What birds do you think we might see today?
What sounds might we hear?
Today, you get to be bird watchers. That means sitting very quietly and looking carefully.
Sit as still and quiet as you can. Nobody talks for one minute.
How many different bird sounds did you hear? Show me on your fingers.
Now use your eyes. Where are the birds? In the hedge, on the ground, or in the sky?
When you see one, freeze, and point with your chin, not your arm. Birds fly from arms.
Found one? Tick it on your sheet. If it is not on the sheet, sketch it.
The birds we see most in winter are the ones that stay all year: the robin, the blue tit, the blackbird and the wood pigeon.
Come into a circle, and stand still. Both feet on the ground.
Voices down. Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, and keep hold of it.
Let that sound go. Eyes back to the circle.
What was the furthest sound you heard?
What is the highest thing you can see from here?
What do you think birds find hard to find in winter?
How could we help them?
Today we are going to build our own bird feeder.
Draw your feeder first. Where is the hole? Where does the bird stand?
Label what you will use: bottle, spoon, string, seed.
Check it against your drawing. Is it the feeder you designed?
Where should it go? Somewhere a cat cannot reach, and a little away from the windows.
Hang it up. Now step back and give the birds some quiet.
A feeder needs looking after. We will clean ours out every couple of weeks, so mould cannot build up.

What do you think tree bark feels like?
Do you think every tree's bark looks the same?
Today we are going to make bark rubbings to find out.
Every tree wears its own coat. Is this one rough or smooth? Bumpy or cracked?
Does this one feel rougher or smoother than the last?
Hold your paper flat against the bark and rub gently with the side of your crayon.
When the pattern is there, write which tree it came from on the paper.
Wet bark will not share its pattern with paper, but dry things will. Find the dry side of the big trees, or bring a fallen stick or a leaf under our shelter and rub that instead.
Lay all the rubbings out together, pattern facing up.
Bark protects a tree, much like skin protects us.

What do animals need in winter that is hard to find?
How do you think animals stay safe and warm?
Animals have three ways to get through winter. Hibernate: sleep through it, like a hedgehog.
Migrate: fly somewhere warmer, like a swallow.
Adapt: grow thicker fur or feathers and stay, like a robin.
Can you spot any signs of squirrels, birds, or a place an animal might hibernate?
Sort your cards into three piles: hibernate, migrate, adapt.
Now we go through them together. Hold up your hedgehog. Which pile?
Hedgehogs, dormice and bats really hibernate. Squirrels only slow down. Swallows fly all the way to Africa, and robins stay and fluff up.

What does a thing have to do before we call it alive?
A tree never walks anywhere. Is a tree alive?
We have three groups today. Alive. Dead. Never alive.
Dead is the tricky one. Dead means it was alive once, or part of something alive, and it has stopped.
Two things on each tray. One you think is dead. One you think was never alive.
If you find something alive, leave it exactly where it is. Draw it on a card, and bring the card back.
Put each thing, and each card, in the circle where you think it belongs.
Now walk round. If you disagree with something, move it, and be ready to say why.
Hold up the one that was hardest to place. Tell us what decided it.
Living things grow and feed, and their kind makes more of itself. Dead things were alive once, or part of something alive. Never alive things never were.

A habitat is the place something lives. A micro-habitat is a tiny one inside it.
Under one stone. Inside one rotting log. In one crack in a wall.
We are going to open three small places, and put every one of them back.
Kneel down first. You cannot look into a small place from standing up.
Count first. How many different kinds are living in there?
Now open a rotting one. Then find a crack, or a tuft of grass, and open that.
Choose one creature. Count the legs. Look for wings.
If you do not know its name, describe it well enough that somebody else could find it.
Now choose one plant growing in your small place itself, in the crack or under the edge. Look at the shape of its leaves.
Now put everything back where it came from, and the stone back the way it was.

What would you need if you had to live out there all year?
Animals need air, water and food. Most of them need somewhere to shelter too.
Plants need light, air and water, and somewhere to grow. Many of them grow roots into soil.
A habitat is a place that gives the things living there what they need.
Lay your string round your patch. Everything inside it is yours to study.
Write what you can actually see, not what you think ought to be there.
Find a living thing in your patch that needs another living thing.
Does the need go both ways, or only one way?

The chains we build today start with a green plant. A plant makes its own food out of light.
An animal that eats only plants is a herbivore.
An animal that eats animals but not plants is a carnivore. An animal that eats both plants and animals is an omnivore.
When one animal hunts another, the hunter is the predator and the hunted one is the prey.
We are going to build a chain today out of things we have actually found, and nothing else.
Find a plant first. Then find something that has been eating it.
A hole in a leaf tells us something may have eaten it. It does not tell us what.
Now look up. Is there anything out here that would eat the eater?
The arrow points at whoever is doing the eating, because that is where the food goes.
